title: Hifz Tracker
subtitle: A method and tracking grid for Qur'an memorization
intro: Memorizing the Qur'an (hifz) is a lifelong commitment that rewards consistency more than intensity. This sheet gives you a simple, repeatable method along with a tracking grid and validation steps so every new page becomes a lasting page.

sections.heading: The 5-step daily method
sections.body: Apply these steps to each new page (wajh) before moving on.
bullets: 1. Listen: play a trusted reciter's recitation of the page 3-5 times while following the muṣḥaf.
2. Read aloud: repeat each verse yourself, correcting pronunciation against the recording.
3. Memorize line by line: repeat each line 10-15 times, then link it to the previous line.
4. Consolidate the page: recite the full page from memory 5 times without looking.
5. Test: recite to a teacher, family member, or record yourself and self-check against the muṣḥaf.

rows: Consolidation of the week's pages (murajaʿa qariba)
5-10 min review of older juzʾ (murajaʿa baʿida)

sections.heading: Validation levels
bullets: Level 1 - Rough: recited with hesitation, teacher corrects several words.
Level 2 - Fluent: recited without stopping, minor tajwīd notes only.
Level 3 - Solid: recited perfectly twice on two different days.
Level 4 - Anchored: recited correctly after 30 days without specific review.

sections.heading: Common obstacles and solutions
bullets: Forgetting quickly: increase murajaʿa frequency, not just new memorization.
Mixing up similar verses: use a tashabuh (resemblance) notebook to list look-alike ayat.
Loss of motivation: memorize in a group or with an accountability partner.
Poor pronunciation locking in errors: never memorize a page before correcting its recitation.

sections.heading: Qur'anic example: gradual revelation as a model

arabicExamples.ar: وَقُرْآنًا فَرَقْنَاهُ لِتَقْرَأَهُ عَلَى النَّاسِ عَلَىٰ مُكْثٍ وَنَزَّلْنَاهُ تَنزِيلًا
arabicExamples.translit: wa Qur'anan faraqnahu litaqra'ahu 'ala an-nasi 'ala mukthin wa nazzalnahu tanzila
arabicExamples.note: Al-Isra 17:106 - the Qur'an was revealed gradually; memorization should follow the same wisdom of patience and pacing.

sections.heading: Monthly review checklist
bullets: Recite the entire month's new pages from memory without error.
Test at least 3 random pages from earlier juzʾ.
Note recurring tajwīd mistakes and target them specifically next month.
Set the next month's page target based on this month's actual pace, not an ideal one.

practice.heading: Practice
lines: Fill in the tracking grid daily, even if only one line was memorized.
Record yourself weekly and compare to a certified reciter.
Never move to a new page until the previous one reaches Level 2.

title: Makharij al-Huruf
subtitle: The articulation points of the Arabic letters
intro: Makharij al-huruf are the precise points in the mouth and throat where each Arabic letter originates. Mastering them is the foundation of correct tajwīd, since a letter pronounced from the wrong point changes its identity entirely.

rows: The open space of the mouth and throat (for the long vowels)

sections.heading: Al-Jawf - the empty space
bullets: Produces the three long vowel letters (huruf al-madd): alif preceded by fatha, waw preceded by damma, ya' preceded by kasra.
No fixed contact point; sound flows freely through the open mouth cavity.

arabicExamples.note: contains alif and waw madd letters

sections.heading: Al-Lisan - the tongue (10 points)
bullets: Aqsa al-lisan with soft palate: qaf
Aqsa al-lisan with hard palate: kaf
Wasat al-lisan: jim, shin, ya'
Edges of tongue with molars: dad
Edge of tongue with gums (below front teeth ridge): lam
Tip of tongue below lam's point: nun
Tip of tongue with vibration: ra'
Tip of tongue with upper gum ridge: ta', dal, ta' (emphatic)
Tip of tongue near upper incisors: za', sin, sad
Tip of tongue between teeth: tha', dhal, za' (thal group)

sections.heading: Ash-Shafatan - the two lips (fixed)
bullets: Fa': inner lower lip with the tips of the upper front teeth.
Ba', mim, waw: between the two lips (waw with rounding, ba'/mim with full closure).

sections.heading: Al-Khayshum - the nasal cavity
bullets: Source of ghunna (nasalization), present in every idgham with ghunna, ikhfa', and iqlab.
Also the residual nasal sound accompanying mushaddad nun and mim (نّ / مّ).

arabicExamples.note: Iqlab example, An-Naba 78:39 pattern - nun sakin becomes mim with ghunna through the nose

sections.heading: Why makharij matter
bullets: Confusing dad and za' changes meaning: dalla (went astray) vs zalla (slipped).
Confusing sin and sad alters the word's root entirely.
Precise makharij is a prerequisite before learning sifat (letter characteristics).

practice.heading: Practice
lines: Say each letter in isolation, feeling exactly where contact or narrowing occurs.
Pair confusable letters (dad/za', sin/sad, ta'/ta') and practice minimal pairs.
Ask a teacher to check your throat letters (halq) specifically, as they are hardest to self-correct.

title: Correction Journal
subtitle: How to log mistakes, corrections, and self-assess your recitation
intro: A correction journal turns recurring tajwīd mistakes into a visible, trackable pattern instead of vague frustration. By writing down exactly what went wrong and how it was fixed, you build a personalized map of what to focus on next.

sections.heading: Why keep a journal
bullets: Mistakes repeated silently never get fixed; writing them down makes them concrete.
It reveals patterns: the same makhraj, the same rule, the same surah triggering errors.
It documents progress over months, which sustains motivation.

sections.heading: What to record after each session

rows: Makhraj, sifah, madd, ghunna, waqf, rhythm...
What the correct form is, in your own words

sections.heading: Categories of common mistakes
bullets: Makhraj errors: pronouncing a letter from the wrong point (e.g., qaf as kaf).
Sifat errors: losing tafkhim (heaviness) on emphatic letters like sad, dad, ta', za'.
Madd errors: holding a long vowel too short or too long.
Ghunna errors: skipping the nasal sound in idgham, ikhfa', iqlab, or shaddah.
Waqf errors: stopping or continuing at the wrong place, changing meaning.

sections.heading: Self-assessment method
bullets: Record your recitation weekly using a phone or app.
Listen back while following the mushaf line by line.
Mark every deviation, however small, before checking with a teacher.
Compare this week's recording to last month's to hear real progress.

arabicExamples.note: Al-Muzzammil 73:4 - recite the Qur'an with tartil, i.e. slowly and precisely, which naturally invites correction and care.

sections.heading: Monthly review
bullets: Count how many entries moved from 'New' to 'Resolved'.
Identify the single most frequent mistake type and dedicate one week to it.
Celebrate resolved entries by re-testing them a month later to confirm retention.

practice.heading: Practice
lines: Keep the journal open during every recitation session, not just after.
Review the journal before starting new memorization, not only after mistakes.
Share the journal with your teacher monthly for a broader check.

title: Weekly Revision Planning
subtitle: A murajaʿa schedule to protect what you have memorized
intro: Memorization without review fades quickly. This weekly planning sheet organizes murajaʿa (revision) into manageable, recurring blocks so that every juzʾ you have memorized stays fresh and accessible.

sections.heading: Three circles of revision
bullets: Circle 1 - Recent (this week's new pages): reviewed daily.
Circle 2 - Near (last 1-3 months): reviewed 2-3 times per week.
Circle 3 - Far (older juzʾ): reviewed once weekly on rotation.

sections.heading: Rotation method for large hifz
bullets: Divide the memorized Qur'an into weekly portions (e.g., one juzʾ per day for a full hafiz).
Rotate so that every portion is reviewed at least once every 1-2 weeks.
Adjust rotation speed based on how much is memorized: smaller hifz, faster rotation.

sections.heading: Signs a portion needs more review
bullets: Hesitation or pausing mid-ayah.
Needing the first word of the next ayah as a prompt.
Confusing two similar ayat (mutashabihat) from different surahs.
Difficulty starting from a random ayah without going back to the beginning.

arabicExamples.ar: وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ فَهَلْ مِن مُّدَّكِرٍ
arabicExamples.translit: wa laqad yassarna al-Qur'ana lidh-dhikri fahal min muddakir
arabicExamples.note: Al-Qamar 54:17 - the Qur'an is made easy for remembrance (dhikr), which is the essence of murajaʿa.

sections.heading: Adapting the plan to busy weeks
bullets: If time is short, prioritize Circle 1 over new memorization - protect what exists first.
Use commute or wait times for audio-only review (listening while following mentally).
Never skip Friday consolidation; it anchors the whole week.

practice.heading: Practice
lines: Print or copy the weekly grid and fill it in every evening.
Set a fixed weekly rotation day for Circle 3 far-review.
Re-plan the week each Friday based on what actually happened, not what was ideal.

title: Tadabbur
subtitle: A method for meditating on and reflecting over a verse
intro: Tadabbur is the deliberate reflection on the Qur'an's meanings, moving beyond correct recitation toward understanding and internalizing the message. This sheet offers a structured method to reflect on any ayah, with a worked example.

sections.heading: The 5-step tadabbur method
bullets: 1. Read slowly: recite the ayah two or three times with tartil, without rushing.
2. Understand the meaning: check a translation and a brief tafsir summary.
3. Ask questions: Who is speaking? To whom? What is the context (sabab al-nuzul)?
4. Connect to yourself: how does this ayah apply to your life today?
5. Respond: through dua, a change in action, or gratitude.

sections.heading: Key questions to ask every ayah
bullets: What names or attributes of Allah appear here?
Is there a command, a prohibition, a promise, or a warning?
What emotion does this ayah evoke - hope, fear, gratitude, awe?
Does this connect to another ayah I already know (cross-referencing)?

sections.heading: Worked example: Al-Baqara 2:286

arabicExamples.ar: لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا
arabicExamples.translit: la yukallifu Allahu nafsan illa wus'aha
arabicExamples.note: Al-Baqara 2:286 - Allah does not burden a soul beyond what it can bear.

bullets: Meaning: every obligation and trial is calibrated to your actual capacity.
Application: when overwhelmed, remember this ayah as proof you can handle your current test.
Response: a short dua asking Allah for ease in a specific current difficulty.

sections.heading: Worked example: Ar-Rahman 55:13

arabicExamples.note: Ar-Rahman 55:13 - repeated refrain: 'Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?'

bullets: Meaning: a rhetorical question repeated 31 times, listing divine favors.
Application: list 3 specific favors in your own life each time you read it.
Response: say alhamdulillah consciously after each repetition.

sections.heading: Tools that help tadabbur
bullets: A concise tafsir (e.g., Tafsir as-Sa'di or Ibn Kathir summarized) alongside the mushaf.
A reflection notebook to write one line per ayah studied.
Root-word study: knowing the Arabic root deepens the meaning beyond translation.

sections.heading: Common mistakes in tadabbur
bullets: Rushing through many ayat instead of dwelling on one deeply.
Relying only on personal impression without checking established tafsir.
Treating tadabbur as an intellectual exercise without any change in action.

practice.heading: Practice
lines: Pick one ayah daily and apply the 5-step method for 10 minutes.
Write a single sentence of personal reflection in a notebook.
Revisit the same ayah after a month to see if your reflection has deepened.

title: Guide to Waqf Signs
subtitle: Stopping and resuming signs in the mushaf
intro: Waqf (stopping) signs guide the reciter on where a pause preserves meaning and where continuing is necessary. Misreading these signs can distort the intended meaning of a verse, making this one of the most important practical skills in recitation.

sections.heading: Why waqf matters
bullets: Some stops change meaning entirely if placed incorrectly.
The mushaf marks recommended, permissible, or forbidden stops based on scholarly consensus.
Correct waqf reflects understanding of sentence structure, not just breathing needs.

rows: Obligatory stop; continuing would corrupt the meaning
Do not stop here; stopping distorts meaning
Permissible to stop or continue, both equally fine
Stopping is preferable, though continuing is allowed
Continuing is preferable, though stopping is allowed
Stop at one of the two dots only, not both

arabicExamples.translit: wa ma hum bimu'minin ... yukhadi'una Allaha
arabicExamples.note: Al-Baqara 2:8-9 - a stop is required at the end of ayah 8 to avoid merging unrelated statements.
Al-Baqara 2:2 - stopping after 'la rayba' alone could wrongly suggest doubt exists; the full phrase 'no doubt in it' must be read together, or with mu'anaqah dots properly.

sections.heading: How to resume after a stop (ibtida')
bullets: If you stopped mid-sentence, resume slightly before the stop point when meaning requires it.
If you stopped at a complete meaning unit, you may resume exactly where you stopped.
Never resume in a way that reverses or negates the meaning of what precedes.

sections.heading: Practical waqf categories
bullets: Waqf ikhtibari: stopping for teaching/testing purposes at any word, even mid-ayah.
Waqf idtirari: stopping out of necessity (breath, sneeze, forgetting) - resume from the nearest correct point.
Waqf al-qur'an (natural end of ayah): always permissible, marked by the ayah number itself.

sections.heading: Practice recommendations
bullets: Study a mushaf edition with clear waqf signs (e.g., Uthmani mushaf with tajwīd color coding).
Practice on Surah Al-Baqara verses 1-20, which contain multiple sign types.
Ask a teacher to verify your stopping choices on ambiguous ja'iz cases.

practice.heading: Practice
lines: Recite 10 ayat daily, consciously naming each waqf sign encountered aloud.
Keep a small reference card of the 6 main signs until they become automatic.
Record yourself and check whether your natural pauses match the marked signs.

title: Annual Qur'anic Goals
subtitle: Yearly objectives and quarterly milestones
intro: Sustainable Qur'anic growth needs a yearly vision broken into realistic quarterly milestones. This sheet helps you define ambitious but achievable goals across memorization, tajwīd, understanding, and consistency.

sections.heading: Four pillars of yearly goals
bullets: Hifz: how many new pages or juzʾ to memorize this year.
Tajwīd: which rules to master and certify (e.g., idgham, ikhfa', madd rules).
Tadabbur: how many surahs to study in depth for meaning.
Consistency: daily habits to sustain (recitation minutes, murajaʿa frequency).

rows: Q1: 10 short surahs; Q2: 10 more; Q3: consolidate; Q4: full test
Track via daily log, review monthly

sections.heading: SMART goal-setting for Qur'an study
bullets: Specific: 'memorize An-Naba' by March', not 'memorize more Qur'an'.
Measurable: track pages, ayat, or minutes, not vague feelings of progress.
Achievable: base targets on your actual weekly pace from past months.
Relevant: prioritize goals that support your current stage (new memorizer vs consolidator).
Time-bound: assign each goal a clear quarter and review date.

sections.heading: Quarterly milestone review questions
bullets: Did I reach the milestone? If not, what specifically slowed me down?
Which habit had the biggest impact on progress this quarter?
Should next quarter's target increase, stay the same, or decrease?
What tajwīd or memorization mistake keeps recurring and needs focused attention?

arabicExamples.ar: وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ
arabicExamples.translit: wa an laysa lil-insani illa ma sa'a
arabicExamples.note: An-Najm 53:39 - a person only gets what they strive for, reinforcing the value of deliberate, tracked effort.

sections.heading: Annual milestone example: full year plan

rows: Learn idgham & ikhfa' + memorize 5 more surahs
Full juzʾ 30 test + set next year's goals

sections.heading: Keeping goals sustainable
bullets: Leave buffer weeks in the plan for illness, travel, or low-energy periods.
Prefer consistent small daily targets over occasional large sessions.
Revisit and adjust goals every quarter rather than waiting for year-end.

practice.heading: Practice
lines: Write your four pillar goals for the current year today, with numbers not vague hopes.
Set a recurring calendar reminder for each quarterly review.
Share your goals with a mentor or study partner for accountability.

title: Essential Qur'anic Duas
subtitle: Transliteration and meaning of key supplications from the Qur'an
intro: The Qur'an contains supplications made by prophets and righteous believers, preserved as models for our own duas. This sheet collects essential Qur'anic duas with transliteration and meaning for memorization and daily use.

arabicExamples.ar: رَبَّنَا لَا تُزِغْ قُلُوبَنَا بَعْدَ إِذْ هَدَيْتَنَا وَهَبْ لَنَا مِن لَّدُنكَ رَحْمَةً إِنَّكَ أَنتَ الْوَهَّابُ
arabicExamples.translit: rabbana la tuzigh qulubana ba'da idh hadaytana wa hab lana min ladunka rahmatan innaka anta al-wahhab
arabicExamples.note: Aal-'Imran 3:8 - 'Our Lord, let not our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us mercy from Yourself. Indeed, You are the Bestower.'

sections.heading: Dua for this world and the hereafter

arabicExamples.ar: رَبَّنَا آتِنَا فِي الدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةً وَفِي الْآخِرَةِ حَسَنَةً وَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ
arabicExamples.translit: rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanatan wa fil-akhirati hasanatan wa qina 'adhaba an-nar
arabicExamples.note: Al-Baqara 2:201 - 'Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.'

sections.heading: Dua for forgiveness of forgetfulness or error

arabicExamples.ar: رَبَّنَا لَا تُؤَاخِذْنَا إِن نَّسِينَا أَوْ أَخْطَأْنَا
arabicExamples.translit: rabbana la tu'akhidhna in nasina aw akhta'na
arabicExamples.note: Al-Baqara 2:286 - 'Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake.'

sections.heading: Dua of Prophet Ibrahim for righteous offspring

arabicExamples.note: As-Saffat 37:100 - 'My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.'

sections.heading: Dua of Prophet Yunus in distress

arabicExamples.ar: لَّا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا أَنتَ سُبْحَانَكَ إِنِّي كُنتُ مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ
arabicExamples.translit: la ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu mina az-zalimin
arabicExamples.note: Al-Anbiya 21:87 - 'There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers.'
Al-Isra 17:24 - 'My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small.'
Taha 20:114 - 'My Lord, increase me in knowledge.'

sections.heading: How to use these duas daily
bullets: Memorize one dua per week alongside its meaning, not just the sound.
Use them in daily salah supplications (after tashahhud or in sujud).
Reflect on the context of each dua (who said it, in what situation) to deepen sincerity.
Teach them to children as short, meaningful memorization pieces.

practice.heading: Practice
lines: Choose one dua and recite it 10 times daily for a week until memorized.
Write the meaning in your own words in a personal dua notebook.
Use the dua of Prophet Yunus specifically during moments of distress or difficulty.
